archetype.name: Rebuilding (young core, record ahead of play)
archetype.definition: A team still building around young centers like Macklin Celebrini, Will Smith and Michael Misa, whose .500 start rests on one-goal wins rather than on controlling games, which it has not done.

report.headline: A .500 start covering for the league's second-worst chance share
report.take:
San Jose is 3-3-0 and fifth in the Pacific, which reads like a team treading water. The underlying numbers describe a team that is being run over. Its 5-on-5 expected-goals share of 37.3% ranks 31st of 32, its shot-attempt share is 25th, and it has been outscored 23-16. The site ranks it 26th, and all three of its roster groups grade D or worse. This is still a rebuilding club, not a bubble team that has hit a slow patch.

The record comes from game margins, not from the overall run of play. All three wins were by a single goal: 4-3 over Florida, 5-4 over Los Angeles, 3-2 at St. Louis. The losses were 0-5 at Dallas, 1-3 to Edmonton and 3-6 to Boston. That split explains a Pts vs Goal Diff of +1.5, fourth in the league. It is a familiar pattern. Last season's 39-35-8 came with a +6.1 on the same measure, a record well ahead of a team the site ranked 27th.

The numbers also hide two things. First, the team has been unlucky at 5-on-5 even while lucky in the standings. A PDO of 91.5 is far below average, Yaroslav Askarov has saved only .848 across five starts, and some of that will correct. Second, Celebrini is the whole show when he plays. He has 8 points and a 7.3 Game Score in only four of the six games, and he is the only regular above even in +/-. The rest of the forward group is bleeding chances: Smith, Stenberg, Chernyshov and Misa all sit at or below roughly 33% xGF. On the blue line, Kesselring logs 19.5 minutes a night while ranking 213th of 239 defensemen.

The direction depends on which correction arrives first. Save percentage and shooting luck should rise toward normal, which helps. One-goal fortune should fade, which hurts. The chance share is the real problem, and it is worse than last season's 47.6%, not better. Expect a team that loses more often than it wins and stays well short of the playoff line.

strengths.title: Celebrini drives everything he touches
strengths.body: In four games Celebrini has 8 points, half of them on the power play, and a 7.3 Game Score that dwarfs every teammate's. His 45.4% xGF is still below even, but on this roster that counts as the best possible result for a top center playing over 21 minutes a night. He is the reason the team can steal close games, and that should last as long as he is in the lineup.

strengths.title: A power play that cashes in
strengths.body: San Jose converts 23.5% of its chances, 10th in the league, which is a meaningful step up from last season's 21.2%. Celebrini, Stenberg and Smith carry it. With 5-on-5 play this lopsided, special teams are the most realistic path to goals. The rate may cool, but the personnel make it at least league-average.

concerns.title: Getting badly out-chanced at even strength
concerns.body: A 37.3% expected-goals share is near the bottom of the league and well below last season's already poor 47.6%. Most regulars are in the low 30s individually, and Nurse, Kesselring and Cagnoni are all around 30-35% while playing big minutes. Six games is a small sample, but a gap this wide does not come from bad bounces; it reflects a team spending most of its time in its own end.

concerns.title: A record propped up by one-goal wins
concerns.body: The Pts vs Goal Diff of +1.5 ranks fourth in the league while the goal differential ranks 27th. Every win has been by one goal and every loss by two or more. Close-game results tend to even out over a season. Last year's +6.1 shows this team has leaned on it before, without becoming any better at controlling games.

concerns.title: Askarov's save percentage
concerns.body: Askarov has a .848 save percentage and -2 GSAx through five starts, and the goaltending grade is a D-. Nedeljkovic's one start (+1.8 GSAx) was better, though that is a single game. Goaltending was this franchise's sore spot last year too, at -25.7 team GSAx. Askarov should improve from here, but the team cannot count on its goalie to cover for its chance share.

trend.note: Wins and losses have alternated in twos, with three narrow wins against three clear losses. The last two games, against Edmonton and Boston, were both losses.

weekAhead.headline: Five-game eastern road trip, with a Toronto-Montréal back-to-back
weekAhead.body:
San Jose spends the whole week away, at Nashville, Detroit, Toronto, Montréal and Ottawa. The Toronto and Montréal games come on consecutive nights. On paper the first two are the softest: Nashville ranks 24th on the site and Detroit 25th, and both are weak at even strength. Those are the games this team has to take, because it rarely controls the run of play anywhere.

The back half is harder. Toronto's penalty kill has allowed almost nothing and its goaltending has been strong. Montréal has the shot-attempt and expected-goals shares to pin the Sharks in their zone. Ottawa has the best record of the five and a B+ goaltending group. A long road trip for a team at 37% xGF is a tough setup even against a mid-table schedule. Two wins would be a fair result.

keyMatchups.title: Power play versus Detroit's leaky kill
keyMatchups.body: Detroit kills only 66.7% of its penalties, 28th in the league, and allows the third-most points relative to expectation to centers. San Jose's 10th-ranked power play, run through Celebrini and Smith, has its best scoring opportunity of the week here.

keyMatchups.title: Toronto's wall on the penalty kill
keyMatchups.body: Toronto kills 95.8% of its penalties, best in the league, and its goalies are at +4.9 GSAx. That shuts off the one area where San Jose has been effective. Toronto is also stingy against forwards, so the Sharks will need to win at 5-on-5, which they have not done.

keyMatchups.title: Montréal's puck control, second night
keyMatchups.body: Montréal holds 54.9% of expected goals and 55% of shot attempts, and it gets the Sharks on the second night of a back-to-back. Its defense has given up the most points relative to expectation to defensemen in the league, a chance for Trouba and Cagnoni to contribute. Even so, a long night in the defensive zone is the likelier story.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the team gets results in Nashville and Detroit before the Toronto-Montréal back-to-back, and who starts in goal on those two nights.

restOfSeason.body:
Two corrections pull in opposite directions. A 91.5 PDO and an .848 save percentage from the starter are far below normal and should rise, which will turn some current blowouts into closer games. The one-goal luck behind the +1.5 Pts vs Goal Diff should fade over a full season. What is unlikely to fix itself is the chance share: a team at 37% xGF, with a D blue line and D- goaltending, will not suddenly play winning hockey.

The realistic picture looks like last year's team or slightly worse. It should be competitive on nights when Celebrini and the power play carry it, outshot on most others, and finish in the bottom third. The growth worth tracking is individual: Celebrini's production, and whether Smith, Misa, Stenberg and Chernyshov can lift their chance numbers from the low 30s.
swingFactors: Whether the young forwards improve their 5-on-5 chance share

confidence.note: Six games is a small sample, but the chance-share gap is too wide to be noise.
